title: One holy catholic church
hook: small c: universal; every tradition says it in its own sense

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Paraclete, the one called to stand beside you. Your line was the comforter comes. Who did you stand beside? Day three hundred six.

Picture a Sunday morning in a Methodist church in Georgia, or a Lutheran church in Minnesota, or an Anglican church in Kenya. The congregation stands to say the creed. And they come to a line that makes some visitors blink: I believe in the holy catholic church. Catholic? Aren't we Methodists? Lutherans? Anglicans? Meanwhile, across town, at a Catholic parish, people are saying almost the same words. And at the Orthodox church down the road, they say: one holy catholic and apostolic church. Everyone is saying catholic, and not everyone means the same thing by it. Today's word is small c catholic, one of the oldest words Christians use about themselves, and it's older and bigger than any one church's name.
screen: `METHODISTS SAYING CATHOLIC.` → `EVERYONE SAYS IT.` → `NOT EVERYONE MEANS THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Catholic comes from the Greek katholikos, from kath' holou, according to the whole. Whole, entire, universal. The first surviving Christian use is in a letter by Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, written on his way to martyrdom in Rome, around the year 110. He says, roughly: wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the catholic church. The whole church, not just one local gathering. About two and a half centuries later, Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, explained it to people preparing for baptism. The church is catholic, he said, because it spreads through the whole world; because it teaches the whole faith; because it gathers every kind of person, rulers and ruled, learned and unlearned; and because it heals every kind of sin. A monk named Vincent, in the 400s, gave a famous test, in Latin: quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est. What has been believed everywhere, always, by everyone. So when Christians today say catholic, they mean it in their own sense. Roman Catholics mean the church in communion with the pope, where they believe the fullness of the church is found. Orthodox Christians mean the fullness of faith present in each local church gathered around its bishop. Many Protestants mean the universal church of all believers, in every place and time, whatever their denomination. Luther's German version of the creed even said Christian church, instead of catholic, to make that meaning plain. They differ on what the word points to. But they all refuse to shrink it: nobody wants a church that's only for one country, one class, or one kind of person.
screen: `KATH' HOLOU: ACCORDING TO THE WHOLE.` · `IGNATIUS, AROUND 110.` · `EVERYWHERE, ALWAYS, BY EVERYONE.` · `EACH CHURCH, ITS OWN SENSE.` · then, large: `ONE HOLY CATHOLIC AND APOSTOLIC CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your local church. Settle, and breathe. Think of the church nearest you, any church, the one you pass on the way to work or the one you grew up in. Picture its doors, its people on a Sunday. Then widen the picture: that church, and all the others on your street, in your town, in your country, around the world. Every kind of person. If you pray, you can pray for that one local church, and through it, for the whole. If you don't, just hold the picture: one little building, and the whole wide world. The bell holds the time.
Catholic. Small c: from the Greek for according to the whole. Universal: the whole church, everywhere, every kind of person.
Your line: universal. Today, notice the edges of your own circle, and let in one person who's usually outside it. Day three hundred six.

howItsDone: Christians of many churches say "one holy catholic and apostolic church" in the Nicene Creed or "the holy catholic church" in the Apostles' Creed, each understanding the word in their own tradition's sense.

options: because it is ruled from one city.

trapdoor: what you thought: catholic means Roman Catholic.
what it means: small c, universal. every church that says the creed says it, each in its own sense.
what a scholar hears: kath' holou; Ignatius's letter to the Smyrnaeans; and Vincent of Lérins's everywhere, always, by all.
